question: Which thread is the bottleneck of batch_server?

trace.classification: Linux kernel trace or an experiment containing a Linux kernel trace

findings.claim: Process 200393 (batch_server) had 6 live thread(s) here: TID 200393 (batch_server) running 0.1%, waiting for a CPU 0.0%, blocked 98.1%; TID 200410 (worker-0) running 5.5%, waiting for a CPU 11.7%, blocked 82.8%; TID 200411 (worker-1) running 5.4%, waiting for a CPU 12.9%, blocked 81.7%; TID 200412 (worker-2) running 5.4%, waiting for a CPU 12.4%, blocked 82.2%; TID 200413 (worker-3) running 5.4%, waiting for a CPU 13.1%, blocked 81.4%; TID 200414 (flusher) running 0.0%, waiting for a CPU 1.8%, blocked 98.2%.

Who woke the threads of batch_server after their waits: TID 200410 waited 497003.629 ms in total (6529 waits) until woken by TID 200393 (batch_server); TID 200411 waited 490125.042 ms in total (6529 waits) until woken by TID 200393 (batch_server); TID 200413 waited 488760.730 ms in total (6529 waits) until woken by TID 200393 (batch_server); TID 200412 waited 331899.355 ms in total (6529 waits) until woken by TID 200393 (batch_server); TID 200414 waited 327331.744 ms in total (6529 waits) until woken by TID 200393 (batch_server); TID 200393 waited 327126.142 ms in total (6529 waits) until woken by a timer (sleep or timeout); TID 200393 waited 261973.629 ms in total (6528 waits) until woken by TID 200412 (worker-2); TID 200414 waited 261775.880 ms in total (6528 waits) until woken by a timer (sleep or timeout).
caveats: This lists every thread's waits, including waits for new work (idle time), so the thread that ends the most waits here is not necessarily the bottleneck; see process.bottleneck.

A wake-up names the thread that ended the wait (e.g. released the lock or posted the data), not necessarily the whole chain behind it; wake-ups across CPUs or from interrupt context can be unattributed or attributed to the idle task.

findings.claim: Following the main thread TID 200393 (batch_server), whose waits are the process's progress: 100.0% of its waiting on other threads (261973.629 ms over 6528 waits) ended with a wake-up from TID 200412 (worker-2), so TID 200412 is the bottleneck. Wait chain, aggregated over those waits: batch_server (TID 200393) <- worker-2 (TID 200412, per wait on average: running 4.663 ms, waiting for a CPU 10.753 ms, blocked 24.703 ms in futex until woken by TID 200414 (flusher)) <- flusher (TID 200414, per wait on average: running 0.012 ms, waiting for a CPU 0.007 ms, blocked 24.684 ms in clock_nanosleep until woken by a timer (sleep or timeout)) <- a timer (sleep or timeout).

chain.name: worker-2
chain.summary: per wait on average: running 4.663 ms, waiting for a CPU 10.753 ms, blocked 24.703 ms in futex until woken by TID 200414 (flusher)

chain.name: flusher
chain.summary: per wait on average: running 0.012 ms, waiting for a CPU 0.007 ms, blocked 24.684 ms in clock_nanosleep until woken by a timer (sleep or timeout)

caveats: Follows the main thread (TID = PID), whose waits are the process's progress; other threads' waits for new work are idle time, not delay, and are not counted here.
Each step of the chain is aggregated over all the waits it explains, so it shows what usually happens, not one particular wait; the example critical path shows one.

findings.claim: If TID 200412 (worker-2) no longer waited until woken by TID 200414 (flusher) (24.703 ms per wait, in futex), the main thread's waits would shrink from 40.131 ms to about 18.434 ms on average (2.2x faster): each would then end when the other threads finish their work (18.003 ms in, on average). TID 200414 (flusher) spent that time in clock_nanosleep, so it most likely holds the lock TID 200412 waits for while it sleeps; not sleeping (or doing slow work) while holding the lock would remove this wait.
caveats: An estimate from this trace, assuming everything else in each round stays as recorded; only re-tracing after the change measures it.
The round cannot end before the threads outside the chain finish their work, so that time bounds the gain (it did in 5180 of 6528 waits).

findings.claim: Example: the main thread's longest wait on TID 200412. Critical path of TID 200393 over this gap, in time order: TID 200412 (worker-2) PREEMPTED 8.453 ms, RUNNING 2.404 ms -> TID 200414 (flusher) TIMER 29.153 ms, PREEMPTED 0.863 ms, RUNNING 0.008 ms -> TID 200412 (worker-2) PREEMPTED 0.003 ms, RUNNING 0.007 ms. Direct waker (last other thread before TID 200393 resumed): TID 200412 (worker-2). Longest activity the wait depended on: TID 200414 (flusher) in state TIMER for 29.153 ms.

TMLL (Trace Server syscall tables) for the bottleneck TID 200412 (worker-2): futex waits: 6,528, 161308.720 ms in total (longest 30.030 ms, 2 distinct lock address(es)); most frequent system calls: futex x16689 (330872.114 ms), rseq x1 (0.000 ms), set_robust_list x1 (0.000 ms), rt_sigprocmask x1 (0.000 ms), prctl x1 (0.000 ms).
caveats: These cover the whole trace, including the thread's waits for new work; the wait chain in process.bottleneck gives the part spent while the main thread waited on it.

findings.claim: TMLL's z-score flagged 3 of the main thread's 6528 waits on TID 200412 as outliers (median 40.046 ms, max 40.890 ms): the delay comes in spikes, e.g. 40.685 ms at 50723.265 ms; 40.890 ms at 192107.380 ms; 40.688 ms at 521930.595 ms.

documents.title: Critical Path (Process Wait Analysis)
documents.text:
Title: Critical Path (Process Wait Analysis)
Domain: trace_compass

# Critical Path (Process Wait Analysis)

Trace Compass can recover the wait causes of local and distributed processes
using operating system events. The analysis highlights the tasks and devices
causing a process to wait, by following the chain of scheduling and wake-up
events backward through however many other threads -- and, when traces from
multiple machines are combined with clock synchronization, however many other
hosts -- are causally involved.

This is a different question than "what does the Control Flow view show for
this one thread." A single thread's BLOCKED/RUNNING breakdown only describes
that thread's own states; it does not say why another thread's actions
determined how long those waits lasted. The critical path instead answers
"which other threads' work is actually on the causal chain that explains this
thread's total duration" -- the same duration can be dominated by one other
thread doing real work, or by several threads and hosts handing dependencies
back and forth (a classic case for a distributed web application, where a
client's wait may be explained by work done by an application server and a
database server on two different machines).

The corresponding view in the UI is the Critical Flow View: right-clicking a
process in the Control Flow view and selecting "Follow" runs this analysis
and displays the result there, with vertical arrows representing
synchronization and communication between the processes involved.

The critical path is recursive and can span every task running on the
system, so a wide critical path is not itself evidence of a problem -- it
means many threads/hosts happened to be part of the causal chain, not that
all of them are the bottleneck. Identifying which specific participant
dominates the path's total duration still requires looking at how much of
that duration each participant's own segments account for.

Historically, LTTng was developed to trace the Linux kernel and, over time, a number of kernel-oriented analysis views were developed and organized in a perspective.

OS Tracing Overview Perspective

The

 Project Explorer View

 Events Editor

 Histogram View

 CPU Usage View

 Disk I/O Activity View

 Kernel Memory Usage View

The perspective can be opened from the Eclipse Open Perspective dialog (
 Window > Open Perspective... > Other).

This perspective is intended to be used to locate performance issues by observing resource usage.

The perspective can show times resource usage is anomalous. This can help locating the causes of system slowdowns in throughput or response time.

An example can be program that is doing a lot of processing then slows down due to a database access. The user will see a dip in CPU usage and maybe a slight rise in I/O access. The user should consider both spike and slums to be an indication of an area worth investigating.

documents.title: Blocking in futex
documents.text:
Title: Blocking in futex
Domain: kernel_tracing

# Blocking in futex

The `futex` system call supports fast user-space locking and waiting. A thread
blocked in a futex wait is usually waiting for a synchronization condition such
as a mutex, condition variable, or runtime lock.

Futex time identifies synchronization waiting, not CPU starvation. To assign a
cause, correlate the wait with the lock owner, wake-up event, runtime state, or
application-level contention.

documents.title: CPU migration and task placement
documents.text:
Title: CPU migration and task placement
Domain: kernel_tracing

# CPU migration and task placement

A runnable task may run on different CPUs over time. CPU migration and task
placement are scheduler decisions influenced by runnable tasks, CPU capacity,
affinity, wake-ups, and load balancing.

Migration alone is not a bottleneck diagnosis. Look for long runnable
waiting-for-CPU intervals, overloaded CPUs, affinity restrictions, or repeated
short runs that match the observed latency.

documents.title: Runnable time and CPU contention
documents.text:
Title: Runnable time and CPU contention
Domain: kernel_tracing

# Runnable time and CPU contention

A runnable thread is ready to execute but is not currently running on a CPU.
Substantial runnable time can indicate CPU contention or scheduling delay.
Low runnable time does not support CPU contention as the primary cause of a
thread's delay.

documents.title: Linux thread scheduling states
documents.text:
Title: Linux thread scheduling states
Domain: kernel_tracing

# Linux thread scheduling states

Kernel scheduling states distinguish running work from waiting work. A thread
can be running on a CPU, runnable but waiting for CPU time, blocked while
waiting for an event, interrupted, unknown, or not alive.

For diagnosis, blocked time and runnable time mean different things. Blocked
time points to a wait condition such as I/O, a lock, a timer, or socket data.
Runnable waiting-for-CPU time points more directly to scheduler delay or CPU
contention.

documents.title: Blocking in poll
documents.text:
Title: Blocking in poll
Domain: kernel_tracing

# Blocking in poll

The `poll` system call waits for file descriptors to become ready for I/O. It
is commonly used by event loops, network clients, servers, and libraries that
coordinate multiple sockets or files.

A wait in `poll` says the thread was waiting for readiness. It does not name
which application dependency mattered unless the ready file descriptor can be
mapped back to a socket, file, pipe, database connection, or other resource.
